items.question: Per Sect. 7.1, what type of main rotor system and anti-torque design does the BK117 D-3 use?
options: Five-bladed bearingless main rotor with fibre-reinforced composite blades and a Fenestron anti-torque design
Four-bladed hingeless main rotor with a Fenestron anti-torque design (H145 D2 configuration)
Five-bladed articulated main rotor with a conventional open tail rotor
Four-bladed bearingless main rotor with a conventional open tail rotor
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1: the BK117 D-3 is a multi-purpose helicopter utilizing a five-bladed bearingless main rotor system with fibre-reinforced composite blades and a FENESTRON anti-torque design — the H145 D2 instead uses a four-bladed hingeless rotor.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.1.1, through how many doors is the BK117 D-3 accessible in its standard configuration?
options: Six: two hinged crew doors, two sliding passenger doors, and two aft clam shell doors
Four: two hinged crew doors and two sliding passenger doors only
Eight, including two dedicated cargo hatches
Two: only the sliding passenger doors
items.explanation: Sect. 7.1.1: the BK117 D-3 is accessible through six doors — two hinged doors for the crew/front occupant, two sliding doors for the rear passengers, and two aft clam shell doors for the rear compartment.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.1, how is the main rotor blade assembly attached to the main rotor hub?
options: By two bolts each, to hub flanges on a one-piece steel-alloy forged hub/mast
By a single central bolt per blade, on a bearing-mounted hub
By a quick-release pin system requiring no tools
The blades are permanently welded to the hub
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.1/7.8.1.1: the main rotor blade assembly (flex-control-unit plus blade) is attached to the main rotor hub by two bolts each; the hub and mast are a one-piece forging made of steel alloy, with flanges for the five main rotor blades.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.1.1, how is lead-lag, flap and pitch movement of the rotor blades accomplished on the bearingless main rotor?
options: Without mechanical hinges, through the flex-control-unit that is part of the main rotor blade assembly
Through conventional flapping and lead-lag hinges at the hub
Through a fully rigid hub with no blade movement permitted
Through hydraulic dampers mounted externally on each blade root
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.1.1: lead-lag, flap and pitch movement of the rotor blades is accomplished without mechanical hinges through the flex-control-unit, which is part of the main rotor blade assembly — this is the defining feature of a bearingless rotor.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.1.2, what are the two main parts of the main rotor blade assembly?
options: The flex-control-unit and the rotor blade
The hub cap and the swashplate
The pitch link and the mixing unit only
The tension-torsion strap and the blade root fitting
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.1.2: the main rotor blade assembly consists of two main parts — the flex-control unit (flexbeam plus control cuff, both composite fiber material) and the rotor blade, attached to the hub flanges by two hub attachment bolts.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.1.2, what does the control cuff of the flex-control-unit integrate?
options: The elastomeric lead-lag damper, transforming vertical pitch-link motion into a blade angle change
The main rotor hub cap only
The engine oil cooler fan
The tail rotor gearbox output shaft
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.1.2: the control cuff integrates the elastomeric lead-lag damper and transforms the vertical motion of the pitch link into a blade angle change.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.2, how many tail rotor (Fenestron) blades does the H145 D3 have, and how is their pitch angle adjusted?
options: Ten blades, pitch adjusted collectively
Four blades, pitch adjusted individually
Eight blades, fixed pitch with no adjustment
Thirteen blades, pitch adjusted collectively
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.2: the tail rotor counteracts main rotor torque and provides yaw control by adjusting the pitch angle of the ten tail rotor blades collectively; control inputs from the pilot or AFCS are boosted by the tail rotor actuator.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.2, in which direction does the H145 D3's Fenestron tail rotor rotate, as seen from the right side of the helicopter?
options: Counter-clockwise
Clockwise
It alternates direction based on flight phase
The rotation direction is not fixed by design
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.2: the direction of rotation of the fenestron-type shrouded tail rotor is counter-clockwise as seen from the right side of the helicopter.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.2, what mechanism compensates for centrifugal forces on the tail rotor blades?
options: Integrated tension-torsion straps mounting the blades to the tail rotor head
A hydraulic damper at the blade root
A mechanical flapping hinge at each blade
Counterweights installed inside the Fenestron shroud
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.2: the tail rotor blades are mounted to the tail rotor head by integrated tension-torsion straps to compensate the centrifugal forces.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, what is the approximate DC bus voltage when the electrical system is powered by the generators versus the main battery?
options: About 28V DC on generators, about 24V DC on battery power
About 24V DC on generators, about 28V DC on battery power
Both generators and battery supply exactly 24V DC at all times
Generators supply 115V AC; the battery supplies 28V DC
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: when supplied by the generators, the system provides about 28V DC to the airborne electrical system, and about 24V DC when supplied by the battery; the standby battery supplies about 24V DC to emergency equipment.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, which busbar type connects the consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure?
options: SHED BUSes 1 and 2
ESS BUSes 1 and 2
NON ESS BUSes 1 and 2
EMER BUS
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: SHED BUSes 1 and 2 connect consumers of secondary importance that are shed in case of a double generator failure; each is supplied by its MAIN BUS. ESS BUSes carry flight-essential consumers, NON ESS BUSes carry high-load consumers needing both generators/EPU, and the EMER BUS feeds IESI and emergency exit lights.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, which busbar directly supplies the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights, with an alternate supply from the standby battery?
options: EMER BUS, supplied by ESS BUS 2
SHED BUS 1, supplied by MAIN BUS 1
NON ESS BUS 2, supplied by MAIN BUS 2
BAT BUS directly, with no ESS BUS involvement
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: the EMER BUS connects the standby air data and attitude indicator (IESI) and the emergency exit lights; it is supplied by ESS BUS 2, with an alternate power supply from the standby battery.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.9.1, what does the BUS TIE control system connect during normal operation?
options: MAIN BUS 1 to MAIN BUS 2 and to the BAT BUS
Only the two ESS BUSes to each other
The EMER BUS directly to the generators, bypassing the batteries
SHED BUS 1 to SHED BUS 2 only
items.explanation: Sect. 7.9.1: the BUS TIE control system connects MAIN BUS 1 to MAIN BUS 2 and to the BAT BUS; in case of an abnormal electrical condition, the respective BUS TIE opens and separates the affected MAIN BUS from the opposite MAIN BUS and the BAT BUS.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.1, the bleed air heating system is automatically switched off by the FADEC under which condition?
options: As soon as engine power exceeds OEI maximum continuous (i.e. OEI 2 min or OEI 30 sec ratings are used)
Whenever the cabin temperature exceeds 25°C
Whenever both generators are online simultaneously
It is never automatically switched off by the FADEC; only the crew can switch it off
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.1: the bleed air heating system is automatically switched off by the FADEC as soon as engine power exceeds OEI maximum continuous (OEI 2 min or 30 sec ratings in use); it automatically returns to normal function once power reduces below OEI continuous.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.2, under what two conditions is the optional electrical heater active?
options: The bleed air heating system is on, AND demisting is selected (PUSH FOR DEFOG lever fully pushed)
The battery voltage exceeds 26V AND OAT is below 0°C
Both engines are at IDLE AND the aircraft is on the ground
The EPU is connected AND the avionics master switches are OFF
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.2: the electrical heater is active only when the bleed air heating system is on (heating symbol indicated) AND demisting is selected (PUSH FOR DEFOG lever fully pushed); it draws about 40A total (20A per generator).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.2, after switching off the electrical heater, for how long is it recommended to allow the ventilation to keep running?
options: At least 30 seconds
At least 5 minutes
At least 2 minutes
No cooldown period is recommended
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.2: it is recommended to allow the ventilation to run for at least 30 seconds after the electrical heater is switched off.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.3.1, what happens when the PUSH FOR AIR lever is pulled (rather than pushed)?
options: Air from the cockpit is recirculated, instead of outside air from the NACA inlet
Outside air from the NACA inlet is used for ventilation
The bleed air heating system is disabled entirely
It has no functional effect; it is a purely mechanical stow position
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.3.1: when the PUSH FOR AIR lever is pushed, outside air from the NACA inlet is used for ventilation; when pulled, air from the cockpit is recirculated instead.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.10.3.2, what automatically activates the avionics cooling blower?
options: A thermoswitch, depending on the temperature inside the instrument panel
A manual switch on the overhead panel only
The BLD HTG rheostat position
The VENTILATION PAX switch
items.explanation: Sect. 7.10.3.2: a thermoswitch activates the avionics cooling blower automatically depending on the temperature inside the instrument panel.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.8.3, how is the main rotor RPM (NR) sensed for indication purposes?
options: By a sensor in the main transmission, with a backup sensor in the tail rotor transmission
By a single sensor mounted directly on the main rotor mast, with no backup
By GPS-derived groundspeed calculation only
By the FADEC using engine N2 as a proxy, with no independent NR sensor
items.explanation: Sect. 7.8.3: NR (main rotor RPM) is picked up by a sensor in the main transmission and by a backup sensor in the tail rotor transmission, and is displayed on the FND and VMD.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.1, how many axes does the AFCS control?
options: 4-axis
2-axis
3-axis
5-axis
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.1: the helicopter is equipped with a 4-axis AFCS, connected to the 28 V DC power system.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a LEFT press of the cyclic stick's AP/BKUP ON switch do?
options: Simultaneously engages AP1 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by, and tries to recover a fully functional AP1 state by resetting transient failures
Simultaneously engages AP2 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by
Disengages AP1 and AP2 together, then arms back-up SAS
Engages tactical mode (TAC) only
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a left press of AP/BKUP ON engages AP1 and sets back-up SAS in stand-by, attempting to recover a fully functional AP1 state by resetting transient failures. A right press does the equivalent for AP2.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a double forward press of the AP/BKUP ON switch do in flight?
options: Provides quick engagement of the traditional upper modes (ALT, IAS, HDG/TRK) to establish a safe flight attitude, e.g. in case of disorientation
Engages tactical mode (TAC)
Disengages AFCS in two steps
Resets back-up SAS only, without engaging either autopilot
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a double forward press of AP/BKUP ON in flight gives quick engagement of the traditional upper modes (ALT, IAS, HDG/TRK), establishing a safe flight attitude such as after disorientation. A long forward press instead engages tactical mode (TAC).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, how does the AP/BKUP CUT switch disengage the AFCS?
options: In two steps: the first press disconnects AP1 and AP2, a re-press after 0.3 sec disconnects back-up SAS
In a single press that disconnects both autopilots and back-up SAS simultaneously
In three steps, disconnecting AP1, then AP2, then back-up SAS
It only disconnects back-up SAS; the autopilots must be disengaged separately on the APCP
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: AP/BKUP CUT disengages the AFCS in 2 steps - press once for AP1 and AP2 disconnection, then re-press after 0.3 sec to disconnect back-up SAS.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what happens if the cyclic AP UM OFF button is pressed for more than 1 second while airborne?
options: It erases the pre-selected references of upper modes (e.g. ALT.A)
It approximately centers the cyclic stick and pedals
It engages the AFCS recovery function
It arms back-up SAS in stand-by
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: AP UM OFF disarms and disengages all upper modes. Pressed for more than 1 sec on the ground with the autopilot engaged, it centers the cyclic stick and pedals; pressed for more than 1 sec in flight, it instead erases pre-selected upper-mode references such as ALT.A.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.4, what does a double press of the cyclic GTC button do?
options: Engages HEIGHT and HOVER mode
Engages GTC mode only
Disengages all AFCS upper modes
Engages ALT.A mode
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.4: a single press of GTC engages GTC mode; a double press instead engages HEIGHT and HOVER mode.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.7, what happens if the AFCS recovery function is engaged while the helicopter is in a hover?
options: The aircraft will automatically accelerate to 40 KT
The aircraft remains in the hover and only wings-level attitude is captured
The recovery function is inhibited and cannot be engaged from a hover
The aircraft automatically climbs to a safe altitude before accelerating
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.7 CAUTION: when the AFCS recovery function (double forward press of AP/BKUP ON) is engaged from hover, the aircraft will automatically accelerate to 40 KT.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.7, what does back-up SAS provide and where is it implemented?
options: Stability augmentation on the pitch, roll, and yaw axes in case of loss of both autopilots, implemented in the stand-by instrument (IESI)
Full 4-axis autopilot function as a redundant backup to AP1/AP2, implemented in the APCP
Stability augmentation on the collective axis only, implemented in the trim actuator
A fully independent second AFCS computer with its own sensor suite
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.7: the back-up SAS mode provides stability augmentation on pitch, roll, and yaw axes in case of loss of both autopilots, and is implemented in the stand-by instrument (IESI).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.9, what does a STEADY RED indication on an axis of the AFCS strip mean?
options: Total loss of stabilization on the affected axis, requiring hands-on piloting
Minor degradation causing the system to be fail-passive instead of fail-operative
The upper mode is armed and functioning normally
Pilot override action is in progress
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.9: on the AFCS strip, RED steady means total loss of stabilization on the affected axis, requiring hands-on piloting; RED inverse video flashing means manual recovery or the pilot's immediate attention is required.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.9, on the AFCS strip, what does a CYAN inverse-video-flashing indication mean, and what should the pilot do?
options: The upper mode is about to disarm automatically; the pilot shall re-arm it if required
The upper mode has already disarmed; no pilot action is possible
The axis has totally lost stabilization; the pilot must take manual control
The mode is engaged and functioning normally; no action is needed
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.9: CYAN inverse video flashing on the AFCS strip means an armed upper mode is about to disarm automatically, and the pilot shall re-arm it if required. CYAN steady instead means the upper mode is armed (normal operation).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.10, on the AFCS status area, what does a GREY component color indicate?
options: Inactive - either failed but recoverable via the AP/BKUP ON switch on the cyclic, or deliberately deactivated by the pilot
Failed and unrecoverable
Active, but on stand-by
Degraded but still functioning
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.10: GREY on the AFCS status area means the component is inactive - either it failed but the failure can be recovered via the AP/BKUP ON switch on the cyclic, or it was deliberately deactivated by the pilot. RED means failed (unrecoverable), CYAN means active but stand-by, and AMBER means degraded.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.12, when coupling the autopilot to a navigation source via the MFD, what does it mean if the coupling key shows no label at all?
options: Coupling is inactive
The autopilot is coupled to the selected navigation source
The autopilot is armed but not yet coupled
A navigation source fault is present
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.12: the coupling key label is CPL (couples to the selected source), DCPL (decouples), or DISARM (disarms the autopilot) - or it disappears entirely, which means coupling is inactive.

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.2, what is the difference between the HDG+VS and TRK+FPA mode combinations selected on the APCP's HDG-VS/TRK-FPA switch?
options: HDG+VS is the traditional combination, while TRK+FPA is GPS-based
HDG+VS is only available in IFR, while TRK+FPA is VFR-only
TRK+FPA is the traditional combination, while HDG+VS is GPS-based
There is no functional difference; the switch only changes the display format
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.2: the HDG-VS/TRK-FPA rotary switch on the APCP selects between mode combinations HDG+VS (traditional) or TRK+FPA (GPS based).

items.question: Per Sect. 7.3.6.5, why does the back-up SAS function use only one SEMA actuator set (SEMA set No. 1) in the pitch, roll, and yaw axes?
options: For safety reasons
Because SEMA set No. 2 is reserved exclusively for the collective axis
Because SEMA set No. 2 only operates when both autopilots are engaged
Because SEMA set No. 1 has greater control authority than SEMA set No. 2
items.explanation: Sect. 7.3.6.5: pitch, roll, and yaw each have two SEMA actuators, but for safety reasons the back-up SAS function uses only one SEMA actuator (SEMA set No. 1) per axis.
